analysis.one_liner: Repeals ACA limits on physician-owned hospital self-referrals and drugmaker payment disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 25 House members, never received a committee vote and died at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed two Affordable Care Act provisions. One restricted physician-owned hospitals: doctors who own a hospital could no longer use an exception to Medicare's rule against referring patients to facilities in which they have a financial stake, and new physician-owned hospitals could not expand Medicare services. The other, often called the Sunshine Act, required drug, device, and medical supply manufacturers to report payments and gifts to doctors and teaching hospitals, and to disclose physician ownership stakes. Repeal would have restored the looser pre-ACA rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who own or want to invest in specialty hospitals, because the referral limits and Medicare expansion ban would disappear, letting them steer patients to facilities they profit from. Drug and device manufacturers also benefit, since they would no longer have to report payments, gifts, and physician ownership interests to the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Physician-owned hospitals and drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA provision limiting the Medicare exception for physician-owned hospitals, restoring previous law as if the ACA had not been enacted.

Repeals the ACA requirement that drug, device, biological, and medical supply manufacturers report transfers of value to physicians and teaching hospitals and disclose physician ownership or investment interests.
Restores or revives the prior law that the ACA amended or repealed, rolling the rules back to their pre-2010 form.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and other patients, who would again face the risk that a doctor recommends a hospital or imaging or device services in which the doctor holds a financial stake, and taxpayers, since self-referral is associated with higher utilization that Medicare pays for. The public would also lose the public database of industry payments to doctors.

drawbacks.text: Physician-owned hospitals argue they compete efficiently, can specialize in high-quality focused care, and that the ACA restrictions protect large full-service hospitals from competition as much as they protect patients.

Manufacturer payment reporting under the Sunshine Act imposes real compliance costs on drug and device companies, and supporters of repeal viewed it as regulatory burden rather than meaningful transparency.
The bill was drafted as a wholesale repeal with no replacement safeguards, so any restrictions on self-referral or disclosure of industry payments to doctors would have vanished entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gains went to two concentrated groups: physician investors in specialty hospitals and manufacturers freed from disclosure requirements. The costs fell broadly on patients and Medicare, since financial incentives to refer patients to facilities a doctor owns are widely associated with more services and higher spending, and the public would lose the payment transparency database outright. The bill offered no offsetting patient protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, but no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2011 by Rep. Doc Hastings of Washington with 10 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced.
On March 28, 2011 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed; no further action was ever taken.
The bill had 25 cosponsors, 22 Republicans and 3 Democrats, but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and the public are better off because the bill died: the limits on physician self-referral stayed in force and the public database of drug and device industry payments to doctors was never repealed. Physician-owned hospitals and manufacturers did not get the relief they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and Medicare, not physician investors

for.name: Rep. Doc Hastings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the physician-owned hospital referral limits and the Sunshine Act payment disclosure requirements.

for.name: 3 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill, including Reps. Andre Carson of Indiana and Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas among the original cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was first referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee on March 28, 2011 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after its referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was recorded.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican (22 of 25), with a small bipartisan handful of 3 Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Physician-owned specialty hospitals and their physician investors
industries.note: Repeal would have removed the ACA's limits on referring Medicare patients to hospitals in which doctors hold ownership stakes and on new physician-owned hospitals expanding Medicare services. A doctor's financial stake in the facility they recommend is a direct conflict with the patient's interest in the least costly appropriate care.

Repeal would have ended the Sunshine Act requirement to report payments, gifts, and physician ownership interests to HHS, eliminating compliance costs but also removing the public record of the financial ties between manufacturers and the doctors who prescribe and use their products.

Repeal would have allowed physician-owned specialty hospitals to expand and draw profitable, healthier Medicare patients away from full-service community hospitals, increasing competitive pressure on them.
With self-referral limits lifted, physician ownership incentives tend to increase utilization of hospital and ancillary services that Medicare pays for, raising program spending.
